title: TEGRA - Scaling Up Graph Processing with Disaggregated Computing
problem: Graph processing accelerators couple compute and memory resources, leading to underutilization when workloads have varying compute-to-memory intensity ratios. Traditional scale-out approaches are expensive and memory-inefficient.
motivation: Disaggregated architectures can decouple compute and memory, enabling independent scaling and dynamic resource provisioning based on workload demands. CXL provides a practical vehicle for memory disaggregation in large-scale systems.
method: TEGRA separates compute from memory into independent, separately-scalable components connected via a standard called CXL, with processors communicating through message-passing—sending messages to request data and coordinate work. This setup allows the number of active compute resources to adapt to each workload's needs, avoiding the fixed compute-to-memory imbalance that limits traditional accelerators. The researchers simulate the system with gem5 (a detailed computer architecture simulator) to measure memory bandwidth efficiency and performance across diverse graph problems.
key_novelty: TEGRA uses CXL to separate compute from memory in graph processing, and automatically scales compute resources based on each workload's arithmetic intensity (the ratio of computation to memory access).
contributions: TEGRA architecture enabling independent scaling of compute and memory via CXL
Message-passing communication model for disaggregated resource access
Dynamic compute provisioning to match workload intensity
Up to 15% memory bandwidth utilization improvement over coupled accelerators
limitations: Simulation-based evaluation only (no real hardware); CXL latency overhead not fully characterized; scalability to very large disaggregated memory pools not explored.
